summary: Discovery focused on Private VPC deployment options: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, egress/ingress controls, region constraints (EU data residency), routing and IP ranges. Customer has strict egress requirements and prefers minimal public endpoints; interested in Redwood Private (VPC-hosted) for compliance. Agreement to run pilot on dedicated small pool; SE to run network checklist and perf benchmarks.
transcript:
[00:00] Sarah Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sarah from Redwood – I'm the AE on the account. Miguel from our SE team is with me. Tom, Priya, Mark, Lisa, thanks for making time. Quick agenda: understand your infra constraints, talk deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private), networking patterns, and next steps.
[00:18] Tom Reynolds: Yeah thanks, so short background — we're Lighthouse Tech, building a customer-facing recommendations engine. We're evaluating options to host inference. Main constraints: EU data residency, SOC2, and no public internet egress for inference traffic if possible.
[00:35] Priya Patel: Also we have strict firewall rules, everything must be whitelisted IPs and we use AWS across accounts with Transit Gateway and Direct Connect to our colo. We can accept VPC peering, PrivateLink, or VPN — but need details on routing.
[00:48] Miguel Torres: Cool — thanks. Quick clarifying q: when you say no public egress, do you mean no egress to internet at all from the inference instances, or just we can't allow outbound traffic to 3rd party services?
[01:00] Mark Chen: We try to avoid any internet-facing endpoints from resources that touch PII. Ideally the inference plane is inside our VPC with interface endpoints to storage and optionally to Redwood control plane.
[01:12] Sarah Kim: Yeah, got it. So Redwood offers three deployment patterns: Hosted (Redwood-managed, public endpoints), Dedicated (reserved capacity with isolated tenancy in our infra), and Private — which can be either our control plane talking to your VPC via PrivateLink or a fully customer-hosted package in your VPC. For most strict compliance folks the Private option is what we recommend.
[01:31] Lisa Duarte: Can you explain the Private variants? We want to understand whether Redwood needs to peer into our VPC or if we provide endpoints.
[01:40] Miguel Torres: Sure. Two main patterns common on AWS: 1) AWS PrivateLink / interface endpoints: Redwood exposes an interface endpoint that you create in your account — traffic stays on AWS network and we don't need public IPs; 2) VPC Peering or Transit Gateway – where we peer subnets and route traffic directly. PrivateLink is generally simpler and keeps each side in control of their IP spaces. Peering can be higher throughput for heavy traffic but adds route table management.
[02:02] Tom Reynolds: What about cross-region? Our primary workloads are in eu-west-1; we also have backups in eu-central-1. Do you support deploying the inference plane in our region?
[02:12] Miguel Torres: Yes — Redwood Private supports region-local deployments. For EU residency we can provision the runtime in eu-west-1 or eu-central-1 depending on your preference. The control plane can be configured to operate via PrivateLink as well so control-plane metadata doesn't leave region boundaries if you need it.
[02:27] Priya Patel: Ok good. Regarding PrivateLink vs peering, what's the IP requirement? We have limited CIDR ranges and we're trying to avoid expanding too much.
[02:36] Miguel Torres: For PrivateLink you don't need extra CIDR ranges — it's an ENI in your VPC with a set of private IPs; we present you an interface endpoint. For peering you need route entries and space for peering subnets, and you have to ensure no overlapping CIDRs. Peering also requires more ops coordination across accounts.
[02:53] Mark Chen: How do you handle egress for model downloads and S3 access? We keep model artifacts in our S3 — do we need a NAT gateway to pull models?
[03:04] Miguel Torres: There are two options. You can host model artifacts in your S3 with a VPC endpoint (gateway endpoint) so instances pull directly without leaving AWS network. Alternatively, Redwood can host artifacts in our private storage inside your region and we can surface them via PrivateLink. For ECR/container images we can do an ECR repo cross-account or pull via signed endpoints. The goal is to avoid public internet egress.
[03:28] Priya Patel: That helps. Another thing: traffic from our app to the inference endpoint — can that stay internal (no public IP)?
[03:36] Sarah Kim: Yes — if you use PrivateLink or peering the inference endpoint is reachable via internal IPs. For Hosted API that's public. Dedicated can be arranged with IP allowlist but still has public endpoints unless we set up private connectivity.
[03:49] Lisa Duarte: Latency is a concern — our SLA needs sub-150ms tail p99 for small prompts. Will Private deployments meet that?
[03:58] Miguel Torres: We aim for low latency. If we place the runtime in your region and use local networking, p99 should be reasonable depending on instance sizes and batching. For strict low-latency use-cases we recommend dedicated GPU pools sized for your qps and small-batch settings; SE will run a benchmark with your sample traffic.
[04:18] Tom Reynolds: Can you talk about autoscaling? We want predictable latency spikes during morning peaks with bursts.
[04:25] Miguel Torres: We support autoscaling policies on Dedicated and Private. You can configure target utilization, burst capacity, and warm pools. For VPC-local deployments we pre-warm pods and keep a cold-start budget to avoid latency cliffs. Also we support policy-based fallbacks to smaller models if capacity constrained.
[04:42] Priya Patel: Security: we need mutual TLS or mTLS between our clients and the inference endpoints, plus RBAC and audit logs. How are certs managed?
[04:52] Sarah Kim: For Private deployments we can do mTLS using customer-managed certificates; we support ACME or bring-your-own certs anchored to your CA. For control plane auth we integrate with SAML/SSO and can ingest your IdP for RBAC. Audit logs and request tracing are available via our Console and can be shipped to your CloudWatch or S3 destination.
[05:12] Mark Chen: Does Redwood support customer KMS keys for encryption at rest?
[05:17] Miguel Torres: Yes — KMS integration is supported. For Private we can use your CMKs to encrypt model artifacts and runtime volumes. If you need HSM-backed keys we can discuss HSM integrations as part of enterprise deployment.
[05:29] Tom Reynolds: Network data plane question: do inference servers initiate outbound connections to Redwood control plane? That has implications for our firewall rules.
[05:38] Miguel Torres: The runtime does call home for metrics and health checks, but in Private mode we can route that over PrivateLink to a control-plane endpoint inside your network. If you want fully air-gapped, we also have an on-prem package that removes control-plane egress but requires more ops.
[05:55] Lisa Duarte: Any differences in model versioning between dedicated vs private? We want to pin models and do canary rollouts.
[06:02] Sarah Kim: All deployment modes support model versioning and rollouts. Private gives you more control to pin and we can implement canaries within your VPC. The Console still works for observability if you give us the endpoints for metrics ingestion.
[06:12] Priya Patel: Ok let's get specific. What networking artifacts do you need from us to spin up a pilot?
[06:18] Miguel Torres: We'll need: VPC CIDR blocks, subnets you'd like us to use (private subnets), route table screenshots, the security group rules you allow for interface endpoints, list of AWS accounts involved, and whether you prefer PrivateLink or peering. Also a service account/role for cross-account resource provisioning if you want us to help create endpoints.
[06:36] Priya Patel: We can do that. Another constraint: our infra team enforces egress via proxy — does Redwood support proxy configuration for outbound pulls?
[06:44] Miguel Torres: Yes, the runtime can be configured to use HTTP(S) proxies for outbound artifact pulls, though PrivateLink + VPC endpoints is preferable to avoid proxy complexity.
[06:54] Tom Reynolds: What about DNS? We use Route 53 private hosted zones; will PrivateLink endpoints resolve properly?
[07:01] Miguel Torres: PrivateLink uses interface ENIs that you resolve via the AWS private DNS name; we can give you the hostnames and you can enable private DNS to map to the ENI IPs. For peering you'd just use the internal IPs.
[07:12] Lisa Duarte: Any limits around concurrent connections or socket count per instance? We have thousands of small requests per second.
[07:19] Miguel Torres: Limits depend on instance type and runtime config. For high concurrency we suggest larger instance classes and a pooling strategy. We'll run perf tests with your QPS pattern. Also the batching layer can help reduce cost but increases latency slightly — we'll tune per your SLO.
[07:33] Mark Chen: Compliance: we need audit logs for every inference call for a red-team review. Are per-request logs feasible?
[07:40] Miguel Torres: Yes, we can emit per-request metadata (not the payload by default) to your logging sink; payload logging is optional and can be redacted. We can also provide request IDs to tie traces together.
[07:52] Sarah Kim: Quick interjection — Miguel, let's show them a sample network diagram. (shared screen)
[07:57] Miguel Torres: On slide A you can see PrivateLink pattern: control plane in Redwood account, interface endpoint in customer account, runtime in customer VPC subnets, S3 gateway endpoints for model artifacts. On slide B peering pattern: runtime in Redwood-managed VPC peered to customer VPC via Transit Gateway, with NAT for egress isolation.
[08:18] Tom Reynolds: How do you handle IP allowlists if we only allow specific source CIDRs?
[08:24] Miguel Torres: For PrivateLink the calls originate from customer's VPC IPs so your allowlist is internal. If you do peering with Redwood-managed VPC, we can advertise specific subnets as allowed sources. For hosted public endpoints we provide fixed egress IP ranges that you can allowlist, but for strict no-internet policies Private is recommended.
[08:41] Priya Patel: Regarding billing and cost allocation — will traffic across accounts incur cross-AZ charges? We want to understand egress costs.
[08:50] Sarah Kim: There can be data transfer charges depending on the pattern. PrivateLink traffic within same region is typically cheaper than internet egress, but peering/transit gateway has its own costs. In the pricing estimate we'll include rough network cost assumptions for expected throughput.
[09:05] Lisa Duarte: Do you have references of other EU customers who ran private deployments?
[09:10] Sarah Kim: Yes — we have references, including a fintech and a healthcare customer who did PrivateLink with CMKs. I'll include anonymized case notes in the follow-up.
[09:20] Mark Chen: One operational worry: patching and OS level access. Who manages runtime patching and updates in Private?
[09:27] Miguel Torres: For Redwood-hosted runtimes we manage patching. For customer-hosted Private we offer two modes: managed runtime (we operate via a cross-account role to rotate and patch) or customer-managed where you control patching and we provide upgrade artifacts and runbooks. For high-compliance customers we often do managed runtime with stricter SLAs.
[09:47] Tom Reynolds: Is the control plane multi-tenant or single-tenant when using PrivateLink? We care about metadata separation.
[09:54] Sarah Kim: The control plane is multi-tenant but we provide strong logical isolation and can offer a dedicated control-plane for enterprise deals. For most customers PrivateLink + CMK + audit logs satisfies separation and compliance.
[10:06] Priya Patel: Let's talk about network testing. What tests will you run and what do you need from us?
[10:12] Miguel Torres: SE will run an initial connectivity checklist: open the interface endpoint, verify TCP connectivity on port 443, ensure DNS resolves, validate S3 gateway access for model pulls, and run a small throughput/latency benchmark with synthetic traffic. We'll need a test role and some sample payloads.
[10:28] Lisa Duarte: Regarding sample payloads — can we obfuscate PII before sending? We need to keep test data sanitized.
[10:33] Miguel Torres: Absolutely — sanitized payloads are fine. We can also run pure synthetic tokenized workloads to measure raw throughput.
[10:40] Sarah Kim: Timeline — what's your target to go from pilot to production?
[10:44] Tom Reynolds: We'd like a pilot in 3–4 weeks and production in Q1. Budget cycles are next month, so early November decisions would be ideal.
[10:54] Sarah Kim: Sounds good. We'll aim for a pilot kickoff in early November. Miguel, can you own benchmark scheduling?
[10:59] Miguel Torres: Yep, I'll follow up with a 90-minute deep-dive and perf test.
[11:04] Priya Patel: A couple specific firewall Qs: do you need inbound ports besides 443?
[11:10] Miguel Torres: Typically only 443 for PrivateLink/HTTPS. For peering we rely on internal ports; we can give exact ephemeral ranges if you want to restrict further.
[11:20] Mark Chen: How do you handle secrets like model keys or API keys? We enforce key rotation via KMS and role-based access.
[11:27] Miguel Torres: We integrate with IAM and can use cross-account roles. Secrets can be stored in your secrets manager; we also support injecting secrets via encrypted parameters during provisioning. Key rotation is supported; we can automate re-encryption with your CMK.
[11:43] Lisa Duarte: Any caveats for Kubernetes versus bare-metal deployments? We're mostly k8s (EKS) based.
[11:49] Miguel Torres: We support EKS cluster deployments; runtime runs as pods with nodegroup recommendations. For high throughput you might prefer instance-backed pools. We'll share node sizing guidance.
[11:58] Tom Reynolds: Ok let's workshop an example: 200 qps, p95 < 100ms, payload size small. What instance types and cluster size do you recommend?
[12:06] Miguel Torres: It depends on model size and quantization. For a 7B quantized model, maybe 4–8 GPUs for a pilot, we can size more precisely after perf runs. We'll propose a minimal pilot cluster and ramp plan.
[12:20] Priya Patel: For VPC endpoints, do we need to create any IAM roles for the interface endpoint?
[12:26] Miguel Torres: Not for the endpoint itself, but if you want us to provision endpoints cross-account we need a role with limited permissions. Otherwise we can provide the CloudFormation template for you to deploy.
[12:36] Sarah Kim: I'm going to summarize next steps and items we'll send after the call.
[12:40] Sarah Kim: 1) Architecture diagram and PrivateLink vs peering pros/cons; 2) Security whitepaper and SOC2 excerpt; 3) Pilot scope and pricing estimate; 4) SE deep-dive scheduling link + network checklist.
[12:52] Tom Reynolds: Sounds good. Are there any blockers from our side today?
[12:56] Priya Patel: We'll gather VPC CIDR and route table screenshots and make a decision on PrivateLink vs peering by next Tues.
[13:03] Mark Chen: I'll get the SOC2 excerpt to you.
[13:07] Miguel Torres: Great, we'll follow up with the CloudFormation template and a checklist.
[13:13] Sarah Kim: Thanks all — we'll follow up via email with artifacts.
[13:17] Tom Reynolds: Thanks.
[13:20] (call ends)
